I am no expert, so take my opinion with a grain of salt.

First, gaming on a laptop ... ugh. Not optimal unless you fork out the big bucks for a laptop that is made for gaming.

That being said, it is worth your time to do research on the exact hardware specs of the machine for Linux compatibility before you purchase. In general, stay away from Intel integrated graphics, as your frame-rates will suck. NVidia has great Linux support, if you are willing to install their binary driver (supported easily with Ubuntu / Mint: just go to Settings->Driver Manager and install it).

Recommended: Use PlayOnLinux for WINE. WINE by itself will use a single "instance" for your apps. PlayOnLinux will use a separate "instance" for each application (To minimize one app from fscking another). (As I understand it from my tinkering).

  • Back to hardware. Specifically research the WiFi hardware and check compatibility. That seems to be a lingering issue for Linux in general, especially for those cheap WiFi adapters that companies are prone to throw in their machines.

  • Check the sound-card compatibility. Do you require 7.1 surround sound in gaming?

  • Get a solid-state HDD. Check that the motherboard supports 6G SATA, and get a drive to match. Samsung EVO drives are great bang for the buck (tried posting a link to Amazon, but that is a banned domain(!?)). To save a little money, you can choose the cheapest magnetic drive they offer (if configurable) and simply replace it aftermarket.

  • Check your hardware to see if it has additional M.2 ports. I have a Lenovo T440s, and I have 3x SSDs in it (yup!). While not ideal for gaming (video card et al), it makes for a kick-ass general computing machine. While SSDs grow significantly in price the larger the capacity, throwing 2x SSDs in a machine could save you money. If the machine comes with an integrated DVD drive, see if there are aftermarket bays you can swap out for an additional SDD.

  • Check the refresh rate of the LCD. You'll want a fast (< 8ms) refresh rate for gaming (IMHO).

  • Check the supported clock speed of the RAM. And get plenty of it. 8GB minimum. The speed of RAM matters for load times, etc.

  • Custom partition your install. As a general rule, if you are going to hibernate, set the SWAP partition to >= 1.5x your RAM. (8GB = 12GB swap). (There is a lot of debate around this ... this seems to be a general consensus on the issue).

  • Consider partitioning /boot (1 GB is what I'd recommend. I was tired of Linux kernels filling up my boot and having to manually clean it out...), / (root, ~25 GB), /swap (see above) and /home (rest of the drive). That has worked well for me.

  • If you are gaming on-the-go, consider a machine that supports dual batteries. Again, my Lenovo T440s has two batteries in it, and with an extended-life external battery, I get ~10-12 hours of real-world use out of it.

  • Keep the ventilation system dust-free. If you game a lot, use compressed air to clean it out every other month or so. It'll keep your machine running cooler.

Again, my two-cents. Best of luck.

I wouldn't touch Ubuntu for the reasons specified in this thread. The other *buntu flavors (Xubuntu, Kubuntu KDE Neon, etc.) and forks (like Mint, which I recommend as a newbie distro) are acceptable and have the same game compatibility as far as I can tell. I also do not recommend gaming laptops, as they are far overpriced (like more than buying a desktop and netbook) and will probably die in a year or two (unless you really hand out cash for like a Clevo/Sager). Just get a normal laptop and dig up some classics or emulate games to pass the time. As for your points:

  1. Absolutely check first. If you have a model in mind, search for "[model name] linux" to see if people have problems with it. Barring that you may have to go part by part, which can be a pain but it'll help you avoid a headache down the road. From personal experience, I can say Nvidia Optimus is a nightmare to deal with.

  2. As long as you do the Windows install first and leave space for your Linux/shared partitions, you shouldn't have any significant issues. FOSS bootloaders are very good at detecting Windows partitions. If you want to share a partition between Windows and Linux, make it NTFS.

  3. DOSbox works natively with Linux, and so do a lot of emulators (and emulator cores with RetroArch).

  4. You honestly don't need Flash if you don't mind working around it. If you do, you can still install it if you enable the proprietary repo (or Gnash if you prefer a hacky, poorly supported, and abandoned FOSS version).

  5. I dual boot but I rarely touch my Windows partition. I was the opposite when I started, though. It was more an experiment until I really got used to GNU/Linux. When you start to notice the (positive) differences, you'll love it more and more.

1. Look at System76. Their machines ship with Ubuntu on them and all of the hardware plays well with Linux so you can buy with confidence.

  2. Having your OS run off a USB stick seems like it would be slow. I know nothing about Win10.

  3. DOSBox runs natively on linux. I use it daily. If you're short on time try looking at Crossover instead of wine or PlayOnLinux. https://www.codeweavers.com/ It is a commercial paid app, so if that isn't your thing then resort to PlayOnLinux :)

  4. Biggest issues I've had with internet stuff in the past are sites that require IE or Silverlight. Some weird government sites still require IE for whatever reason. Now that Netflix works in Chrome I'm pretty happy.

  5. I believe that there are number of resources available. IRC on FreeNode is a huge one. Also the forums specific to the Linux distribution you choose to run.

Gaming: I'm definitely a gamer as well. Steam has like .. 1800 linux games or something now? Last I checked it was about 1/3 of all Steam games work under Linux. Steam only officially supports Ubuntu and SteamOS so I'd stick with a Debian based OS like those two or variants. Anything that uses apt-get and .deb files should make your life a bit easier.

Humble sells linux games, as does gog.com and itch.io .. so check those places out if you haven't already :)

Edit: Do not get an AMD/Radeon video card. If you're a gamer and new to Linux you want an nVidia with the proprietary driver.

I have some experience. I recommend dual booting Linux Mint and Windows 7 Ultimate. Never install any updates on windows 7 ultimate. That is the "gaming" OS. It is just for steam, games, and the internet. Use Linux Mint for everything else. Hell, Linux Mint will play about half your games, too.

  1. Stick to Intel processors with NVIDIA video cards. Beware the UEFI trap. If your laptop has a 32 bit UEFI bootloader with a 64 bit processor, installing Linux will be nearly impossible. It is best to simply verify that the laptop allows you to boot in "legacy" mode.

  2. No problems with that.

  5. When you follow those sketchy online tutorials, hit the man pages for every single command and really make sure you know what its doing. At first it will be really tedious, but in a few months you'll build that nice foundation of knowledge you need to be a decent home user.

I'll answer your questions as best I can as they are numbered. I don't really game but I use Linux almost exclusively (my job forces me to administrate Windows as well) so take my opinions with a grain of salt. YMMV.

  1. If you're looking for a good gaming experience but want to be mobile build a decent desktop and get a decent laptop. Desktops are just better for graphically intensive programs like games. If you choose to only get a laptop, research the hardware compatibility before you buy. Google the hardware you're looking for and see if it plays nice with Linux.

  2. I'm not sure if this is still an issue since I don't pay particular attention to Windows, but AFAIK Windows 10 does not play nice with dual booting. Also there are privacy concerns, though these issues are being backported to Windows 7/8 and Windows has a bad track record with nuking their old OSs to force compliance with their knew standard. As a continuance of question 1, if you decide to go desktop + laptop I suggest getting a used Thinkpad and upgrading RAM. They can be had for fairly cheap, are Linux compatible, and are workhorses for daily drivers.

  3. I have had limited success with WINE. Once again YMMV. I have had much success emulating SNES, N64, and GBA games in Linux. Since most of the games I enjoy were for those consoles I have been very happy with the options availabe.

  4. When browsing the internet you should have some way of blocking flash and javascript anyway. HTML5 promises to end the need for flash as it is a terrible, antiquated product that has always had serious flaws. That said, most of the content on the internet is Browser/OS agnostic and you should have little trouble doing daily tasks in a Linux environment.

  5. If you choose to dual boot you should install Windows first. During the Linux install it will replace the Windows bootloader with another, likely Grub, and that will manage the boots for both OSs. Linux is considerably different from Windows, but I think it is worth embracing the change. It might take a little time to figure out how to do "simple" things. That's okay. It took a while to learn Windows and if you're trying to escape that environment you should expect some growing pains.

A closing piece of advice, don't use Ubuntu. This is, of course, my opinion but Ubuntu is a mediocre operating system and I dislike when people suggest it. While an OS like Arch or CentOS may be a little to much to ask of a new user, there are alternatives such as Mint or Debian. Don't believe the lies, Debian is not a particularly difficult OS, even for beginners.

Anyway, I hope I could help a little. Good luck with finding an option that works for you.
